text.content: Weapons are categorized by their type and generally follow GURPS damage conventions (e.g., burning for blasters, cutting/impaling for vibro-blades, crushing for blunt trauma). This chapter covers ranged weapons — blasters, slugthrowers, flamethrowers, gauntlet weapons — and their ammunition, modifications, and explosive ordnance. Melee weapons and lightsabers are detailed in @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.9YXkSHXGYI6RwDtb]{Chapter 12}.

Many ranged weapons in the galaxy are highly advanced, firing bolts of superheated gas and plasma powered by standardized, rechargeable energy cells. Others propel solid metal projectiles or explosive payloads. Regardless of their function, a character wishing to build, modify, or break down a weapon must interact with its discrete components.

Core Terms

  • Damage: The Base Damage and Damage Type are dictated by the Receiver/Chamber, with some customized barrels modifying it further. A damage bonus is added into the dice term rather than written after it -- a 1d+1 Receiver with a +2 Emitter is 1d+3, not 1d+1+2 -- and a negative one reduces it the same way, so 1d+1 with a -1 is 1d flat. Where a Receiver deals two kinds of damage at once, as the Sonic Cannon Chamber's 5d energy +3d sonic does, the bonus applies to the first term only: the Emitter shapes the primary beam, and the secondary effect is not what it is focusing.
  • Acc (Accuracy): The sum of the Emitter/Barrel's Acc Mod and the Acc Mod of the integrated Targeting/Optics Module -- those two, and nothing else, set the figure printed on a weapon's line. A Mod may also affect Accuracy, and its Effect says so along with when it applies: an unconditional one such as a Rifled Emitter or a Match-Grade Barrel adds to the weapon's Acc outright, while a conditional one such as a Bipod Mount or a Multi-Optic Scope only applies in the circumstances it names -- aiming, or firing braced -- and is never folded into the printed figure.
  • Range: Dictated primarily by the focusing power of the Emitter/Barrel.
  • RoF (Rate of Fire): Determined by the cycling rate of the Receiver/Action. Where a component lists a range rather than a single figure -- a Gauntlet's Firing Mech reads 1-10 -- that is a ceiling, and what the weapon is loaded with sets the actual rate: dart tubes cycle fast, a rocket tube fires one at a time.
  • Charges Per Shot (CPS) / Shots: CPS is dictated by the Receiver, drawing from the total Capacity provided by the Power Unit / Magazine.
  • Reload: Dictated by the Receiver's feed mechanism, and written as the number of seconds the reload takes followed by a letter for how the ammunition goes in. i means the rounds or cells are loaded individually, so a partly empty weapon can be topped up and the time given is per round; s means the whole magazine, pack or clip is swapped as a single unit for that many seconds regardless of how many shots were left. A few entries read si, meaning either method works. Where a weapon lists turns instead, the reload is slow enough that seconds are beside the point and it occupies the whole maneuver. Reloading takes both hands.
  • ST (Strength): Dictated by the ergonomics and bracing of the Grip/Stock. A few weapons override this: a launcher that clamps onto another weapon uses its host's ST, and a wrist-mounted weapon braces against the vambrace rather than the hand. Where an entry's own line differs from its Grip, the entry governs and its Notes say why. A wielder below the listed ST takes the universal Minimum ST penalty: -1 to skill per point short (see @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.9YXkSHXGYI6RwDtb]{Chapter 12}, Key ST Mechanics).
  • Bulk: The base Bulk of the Grip/Stock plus the added length modifier of the Emitter/Barrel. Shoulder-fired ordnance and wrist-mounted hardware are the exceptions -- the first is carried braced rather than swung, the second adds no silhouette at all -- so their entries list a lower figure than the components would give.
  • Rcl (Recoil): Dictated by the Grip/Stock. Two families sit outside that: kinetic weapons -- slugthrowers, cyclers and disruptors -- kick harder than a blaster on the same frame and read one higher, while flame projectors and other pressure-fed weapons have no recoil to speak of and read 0. The entry's own figure is the one to use.
  • Durability (Dur): The sum of the final Durability of the Grip, Receiver and Emitter.
  • Work each one out on its own first -- its Base Dur Mod × its own material's Dur Multiplier, rounded to the nearest whole number, with an exact half rounding to the nearest even number -- a +5 Receiver in Plasteel works out to 6.5, which is 6 Dur, not 7, while a +5 Stock in Duraplast works out to 7.5, which is 8, not 7 (see Final Component Dur, below) -- and then add the three together.
  • Round each part before adding, never the total afterwards: the Blaster Carbine’s three parts come to 6.5, 5.2 and 3.9, which round to 6 + 5 + 4 = 15 Dur; summing first would give 15.6 and round to 16.
  • Material Limits: Each part is only as tough as the material it is actually made from, so a beskar vambrace does not toughen a durasteel barrel bolted to it.
  • Exclusions: Power units and utility items do not add to Durability.
  • Weight & Cost: Calculated by multiplying component volumes by material density and cost, plus the fixed weights/costs of integrated electronics and power units

Modular Components & Base Materials

To calculate the final weight and cost of a structural component, use the following formulas based on the chosen material:

  • Weight = Volume x Density (Density is lbs/ft^3)
  • Cost = Weight x Cost Per lb. (Round up to the next whole Credit)
  • Final Component Dur = Base Dur Mod x Material Dur Multiplier

(Round to the nearest whole number; halves round to even).

The total weight, base cost, and overall Durability (Dur) of a weapon are the sum of its structural parts (Grip/Stock, Receiver, Barrel). Utility items and power units add to weight and cost but do not add to the weapon’s overall Dur.

  • The market price for components is the base material cost × 2 for Phase 1, Armoury (IQ/Average) -- round the material value up to the next whole credit first.
  • The market price for an assembled weapon is its Base Cost multiplied by every phase its construction requires, one at a time -- see Crafting Phases under Crafting Ranged Weapons. Phase 2 is assembly: ×2 for Armoury (IQ/Average) on a conventional blaster or slugthrower, or ×3 for the family's own Armstech specialty (IQ/Hard) on a bowcaster, flamethrower, launcher or gauntlet weapon. A weapon carrying Silicon then takes Phase 3, Computer Programming (IQ/Hard), a further ×3.
  • Market prices can be inflated or deflated based on location.

That gap between raw material and shelf price is the crafter's labour, not a retailer's margin -- see What the Markup Actually Is in @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}.

Each weapon gets 1 of each component type from each step of assembly (Base, Action, Emitter, Utility, Power Unit), flamethrowers and slugthrowers do not take power units.

Step 1: Grips, Stocks & Mounts

The grip determines how the weapon is wielded, its minimum ST requirement, and base handling.

  • † in the Base ST column: the component is two-handed -- a weapon built on it occupies both hands while readied (see Hands, and What They’re Holding, @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}). Assault Stock, Carbine Stock, Rifle Stock, Heavy Mount and Harness Tank all carry it; every other Base component is one-handed.

Power Packs

A blaster bolt is blaster gas — tibanna — ionized into plasma by the pack’s electrical charge, which is why blaster damage is typed energy (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}). Ammunition for blasters comes in a few standard forms. Reloading a blaster with a fresh pack is a Ready maneuver that takes the listed Reload time.

Anatomy: Each pack is a sealed reservoir of tibanna blaster gas mated to an integrated charge cell. Every shot fired consumes one unit of gas and one unit of charge in lockstep — which is why a single Charges number tracks the pair; there is no separate electric meter.

Construction & prices: listed once in the Modular Components & Base Materials catalog above, with the other Power Units — full and empty, all three sizes — rather than repeated here.

Recharging & Top-Ups:

Charge without gas: A pack can lose charge without firing a shot — ion or EMP hits, months in storage, and powering attachments all drain the cell while the gas sits untouched. Electricity is always free to restore: a power pack takes 1 second per charge to refill when connected to any powered source — a ship’s port, a generator, a charging station — and cannot be used while charging. A vendor may ask a small fee for the service, and the GM may price power itself in special circumstances (rationed districts, survival scenarios), but there is no standing cost for electricity. A recharge re-energizes the cell only; it can never restore spent gas.

Top-ups: A gas top-up refills the reservoir for the gas at its material price × 2 (the fill labor) — 15 CR for a Standard Power Pack, 30 CR for a Rifle Power Pack, 60 CR for a Heavy Power Pack on Standard Tibanna — at any armorer, fuel depot, or starport service bay. A top-up includes re-energizing the cell at no extra charge, because electricity never costs anything. A pack is a durable vessel, like a fuel tank — refilling never wears it out; like any carried item, it can be damaged or destroyed in play (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}).

Value: A used pack is worth its Empty price plus its remaining gas pro-rata at the top-up rate. A merchant reads the gauge.

Crafting Ranged Weapons

Fabricating a custom modular ranged weapon requires mechanical forging, precision milling, and for powered variants, advanced electronic calibration.

Building from a Blueprint: Every item you build -- whether it appears in this chapter’s tables or not -- requires its Blueprint in hand (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}: Blueprints): buy the plan for a catalog item, reverse-engineer it from a Deconstruction, or author an original through the Design Phase. Owning or knowing of an item is not knowing how to make one. A proven plan builds at the baseline; a degraded copy or an unproven original takes its penalty on every Crafting Phase roll below.

Pricing Note: All component and finished-item prices below follow the Construction Markup formula defined in @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10} (General Gear & Currency): each Crafting Phase multiplies the base by the tier of the skill it needs, and the base includes 20 CR per Character Point of any trait the thing grants. Mods, munitions and grenades are priced the same way -- their CP column costs what the mod actually does, read off @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.o2ZbGiux36xwNCw0]{Chapter 14}'s Common Advantages: 5 CP per die of damage a munition deals, 10 CP per Affliction plus 5 more per point of resistance penalty, 5 CP for +1 to Acc, Rcl, RoF or damage (matching Telescopic Vision), 10 CP for an Armor Divisor of (2) and 15 for (3), and half the figure where the benefit only applies in narrow circumstances. Fitting a mod is one phase, Armoury at IQ/Average, so the base doubles.

A Mod Has Two Prices: The figure in a Mod's own table is what it costs to buy one over a counter, and it includes the 20 CR per Character Point of whatever the Mod grants. The figure in a weapon's Construction line is what the same Mod contributes to that weapon's base -- its materials at the ×2 of Phase 1 and nothing more, because the trait is paid for once, in the finished weapon's own price, and would otherwise be charged twice. A Phased-Plasma Modulator is 436 CR on the shelf and 36 CR as a line inside the rifle it is fitted to. Use the counter price when a character buys a Mod loose; use the Construction figure when pricing the weapon it is built into.

Skills Required:

  • Blasters (including Disruptors): Armoury (Blasters) or Armoury (Small Arms) at a default penalty to align focusing arrays, gas chambers, and power cyclers.
  • Kinetic Weapons (Slugthrowers, Cyclers): Armoury (Small Arms) or Machinist to forge and mill barrels, receivers, and mechanical firing pins.
  • Heavy & Exotic Launchers: Armoury (Heavy Weapons) for pressure valves, barrel reinforcement, and loading mechanisms. A dedicated grenade or rocket launcher is tighter work than a heavy blaster and takes Armstech (Explosive Launcher), IQ/Hard, at Phase 1 rather than the ×2 Average tier.
  • Gauntlet Weapons: Armstech (Gauntlet) to fit a launcher, firing mechanism and targeting uplink into a wearable vambrace — the tightest tolerances in personal weaponsmithing, and the reason these are priced at the Hard-skill markup tier.
  • Bowcasters: Armstech (Bowcaster), IQ/Hard, to cut and tension the limbs, seat the magnetic accelerator and balance the quarrel feed. Wookiee bowcasters are built to their wielder rather than to a pattern, and neither Armoury nor the blaster specialties transfer to them.
  • Flamethrowers & Liquid Projectors: Armstech (Liquid Projector), IQ/Hard, for the fuel bladder, pressure regulator and ignition head. The hazard is in the plumbing rather than the electronics, so a blaster specialty does not help.
  • Software Initialization (Silicon): Any weapon constructed with Silicon (targeting computers, electronic scopes) requires a Computer Programming roll after physical assembly to calibrate electronic systems.
  • Crafting Phases: A ranged weapon takes two phases, and one carrying electronics takes three (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}'s Construction Markup), applied in order.
  • Phase 1 -- Component Forging. Milling the grips, receivers, emitters, barrels and stocks. Needs Armoury (Blasters), Armoury (Small Arms), Armoury (Heavy Weapons) or Machinist, all IQ/Average, so it multiplies by ×2; that markup is already in each component's listed price.
  • Phase 2 -- Hardware Assembly. Fitting those components into a working weapon, using the skill for that weapon's family: Armoury at IQ/Average for a conventional blaster or slugthrower, so ×2, or the family's own Armstech specialty at IQ/Hard, so ×3 -- Armstech (Bowcaster), Armstech (Liquid Projector), Armstech (Explosive Launcher) or Armstech (Gauntlet).
  • Phase 3 -- Software Initialization. Applies only to a weapon carrying Silicon. Needs Computer Programming, IQ/Hard, multiplying by ×3.
  • A purely mechanical weapon stops after Phase 2.
  • Rounding: Component weight is Volume × Density truncated to two decimals -- not rounded (a 0.0045 ft³ Assault Receiver in Durasteel is 2.205 lbs, carried as 2.2). Component cost is that truncated weight × the material's Cost/lb, rounded up to the next whole credit, then ×2 for Phase 1, Armoury or Machinist (IQ/Average). A weapon's Base Cost is the sum of its finished components; multiply that by Phase 2, and by Phase 3 where the weapon carries Silicon, to reach Market Cost. See Crafting Phases, above.

Assembly Sequence:

  • Phase 1: Component Forging (Hardware): 1 hour of continuous labor per pound of the final calculated weight. The Roll: a single skill check per component -- Armoury (Blasters), Armoury (Small Arms), Armoury (Heavy Weapons) or Machinist, all IQ/Average. This mills the grips, receivers, emitters, barrels and stocks, and its ×2 is already carried in each component's listed price.
  • Success: Each component is forged flawlessly to spec.
  • Failure: Delicate components warped; 50% of raw materials wasted.
  • Critical Failure: 100% of materials destroyed, crafter takes 1d-3 damage from forge/machining accident.
  • Phase 2: Hardware Assembly: 2 hours. The Roll: the skill for that weapon's family -- Armoury (Blasters), Armoury (Small Arms) or Armoury (Heavy Weapons), IQ/Average, for a conventional blaster or slugthrower, so ×2. A weapon whose family has its own Armstech specialty is assembled with that instead, IQ/Hard, so ×3: Armstech (Bowcaster) for bowcasters, Armstech (Liquid Projector) for flamethrowers, Armstech (Explosive Launcher) for grenade and rocket launchers, Armstech (Gauntlet) for gauntlet weapons. The components are the same either way -- a rifle stock is a rifle stock -- it is fitting them into a working weapon of that family that needs the harder skill.
  • Success: The weapon is balanced and seats cleanly.
  • Failure: Mis-seated. No materials wasted, but another 2 hours of refitting before rolling again.
  • Critical Failure: A component is sprung or cross-threaded and is ruined; it must be reforged.
  • Phase 3: Software Initialization (Electronics): 1 hour of coding, and only for a weapon carrying Silicon -- a targeting computer, an electronic scope, an active chamber. The Roll: Computer Programming, IQ/Hard. A purely mechanical weapon skips this phase entirely.
  • Success: Firmware communicates perfectly with the firing chamber.
  • Failure: Weapon is “bricked.” No parts wasted, but requires another hour of debugging.
  • Critical Failure: Hidden flaw. Weapon functions, but will suffer an automatic Malfunction on its very first attack roll.

Workspace Modifiers:

  • Improvised/Field Tools: -5 to skill
  • Basic Toolkit: -2 to skill
  • Dedicated Workshop/Lab: +0 to skill
  • Advanced Research Facility: +2 to skill
  • Taking Extra Time: As @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10} (General Gear & Currency): double the base time for +1, four times for +2, eight times for +3, fifteen times for +4, thirty times for +5, whatever your tools.

Default appearance. A weapon with no finish specified looks like the material it is made of: Durasteel dull gunmetal gray; Plasteel off-white with a faint sheen; Duraplast matte pale gray; Plastoid bone white; Scrap Metal mismatched, rusted and pitted; Phrik dark silver-blue; Beskar bright polished silver; Wroshyr Wood deep red-brown grain; Electrum warm pale gold; Aurodium rich yellow gold. A weapon built from several materials shows its Base component's finish unless the player says otherwise.

Coloring: Finish is free and changes nothing — no weight, no cost, no Acc, Damage, Bulk or Dur. Improvised/Field Tools and a Basic Toolkit can produce the weapon but not finish it, and it comes out the default shade of its material. The same applies to refinishing a weapon already made. A weapon bought rather than built comes however the player wants it.

Installing/Swapping Components

Swapping a Sight/Optic, Stock/Chassis, Trigger Assembly, Power Unit, or Barrel/Emitter on a fully assembled ranged weapon requires breaking the weapon's outer casing and recalibrating its targeting and firing mechanisms. The removed component comes out intact, retaining its own established Base/Market Cost value for reuse or resale.

Base Time: 30 minutes per component swapped.

Skills Required:

  • Armoury (Blasters), Armoury (Small Arms) or Armoury (Heavy Weapons) for physical and structural components (Stocks, Chassis, Trigger Assemblies, and kinetic feeds/barrels) -- or the weapon's own Armstech specialty where it has one: Armstech (Bowcaster), Armstech (Liquid Projector), Armstech (Explosive Launcher) or Armstech (Gauntlet).
  • Electronics Repair (Blasters) for energy-based components (Power Cells, Emitters, and Ion/Plasma firing mechanisms).
  • Electronics Repair (Computers/Sensors) for Sights, Optics, and smart-targeting uplinks.

Failure: The new component is improperly seated, or the targeting alignment is severely warped. The weapon is non-functional until another 30 minutes are spent recalibrating and realigning it.

Deconstructing Ranged Weapons

While Salvaging is a fast method for reducing a weapon down to its generic raw materials (e.g., pounds of Durasteel or Diatium) for a quick payout, Deconstruction is the meticulous process of breaking a weapon down to preserve its discrete, fully functional modular components. This is ideal for mechanics looking to strip a pristine Heavy Receiver or a highly-calibrated Targeting Module from a captured blaster to install on their own custom chassis.

Recording a Blueprint: A successful Deconstruction is also the moment to record a Blueprint of the weapon (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}: Blueprints) -- a blank Datacard and a Computer Operation roll, made during the teardown. Salvaging never yields one.

Phase 1: Meticulous Disassembly (Physical)

  • Skills: Armoury matching the weapon -- Armoury (Blasters) for the blaster family, Armoury (Small Arms) for slugthrower pistols and rifles, Armoury (Heavy Weapons) for heavy and repeating weapons. A weapon whose family has its own Armstech specialty comes apart with that skill rather than Armoury, the same principle that governs lightsabers in @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.9YXkSHXGYI6RwDtb]{Chapter 12}: Armstech (Bowcaster), Armstech (Liquid Projector), Armstech (Explosive Launcher) or Armstech (Gauntlet). Someone without it may still try Armoury at a -4 penalty, working against tolerances they do not understand.
  • Time: 30 minutes of labor per pound of the weapon’s scaled weight (twice as long as salvaging).
  • Success: Safely extracts one intact, reusable structural component or modification of the crafter's choice (e.g., the Emitter, the Grip, or a specific Mod), retaining its established Base/Market Cost value from the component breakdown above for reuse in a new build. For every 2 points of Margin of Success, one additional intact component may be safely extracted. Anything not extracted intact comes back as raw material separated by type, at 75% of its weight -- 90% on a critical success.
  • Critical Success: Flawless teardown. Every discrete modular component and installed modification making up the weapon is extracted fully intact and ready for immediate reassembly.
  • Failure: A stripped screw, fused plasma channel, or clumsy pry-bar ruins the attempt. The targeted component is warped and rendered non-functional. The weapon is destroyed, yielding only 25% of its base raw material weight in scrap.
  • Critical Failure: A catastrophic mishandling of the weapon's energy gates or pressure valves causes a violent blowout. All components are completely destroyed, and the crafter takes 1d-3 damage.

Phase 2: Firmware Wiping (Electronics)

Any extracted component that natively requires Silicon (such as Targeting Modules, Exotic Chambers, or smart-linked triggers) retains its previous hardware registry and security protocols. It must be scrubbed before it can successfully "handshake" with a new weapon.

  • Skills: Computer Programming.
  • Time: 30 minutes of data-wiping per Silicon-based component extracted.
  • Success: The component's firmware is wiped clean, restoring it to a factory-default state ready for installation into a new build.
  • Failure: The component's anti-tamper software triggers, hard-locking the firmware. The physical component is unharmed, but it cannot be installed until a dedicated slicing attempt (requires an hour and a Slicing or Computer Programming roll at -2) breaks the lock.
  • Critical Failure: The firmware wipe accidentally cascades into the hardware's physical logic gates, permanently "bricking" the Silicon node. The component is rendered completely useless.

Salvaging Ranged Weapons

Breaking down captured, damaged, or obsolete ranged weapons allows characters to reclaim valuable raw materials, silicon components, and delicate arrays.

Phase 1: Disassembly & Extraction

  • Skills: Armoury matching the weapon -- Armoury (Blasters), Armoury (Small Arms) or Armoury (Heavy Weapons) -- and Computer Programming for Silicon extraction. A weapon whose family has its own Armstech specialty comes apart with that skill rather than Armoury, the same principle that governs lightsabers in @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.9YXkSHXGYI6RwDtb]{Chapter 12}: Armstech (Bowcaster), Armstech (Liquid Projector), Armstech (Explosive Launcher) or Armstech (Gauntlet). Someone without it may still try Armoury at a -4 penalty, working against tolerances they do not understand.
  • Time: 15 minutes of labor per pound of the weapon’s scaled weight.
  • Success: Safely strips the weapon, recovering 50% of its original raw material weight. A Critical Success recovers 75% and preserves a fully intact, reusable modification.
  • Failure: The weapon is clumsily stripped. Delicate lenses crack, metal warps, and the yield is 0. A Critical Failure means a power cycler overloads or spring snaps, destroying all materials and inflicting 1d-3 damage to the salvager.
  • Software Failure: Failing the Computer Programming roll specifically “bricks” the electronics. Physical scrap can still be salvaged via Armoury, but no Silicon weight is recovered.

Crafting Ammunition (Power Packs, Projectiles, and Fuel)

This system governs the fabrication, calibration and chemical mixing required to produce usable ammunition, from standard blaster power cells to specialized slugthrower rounds and volatile incendiary fuels.

Building from a Blueprint: Every item you build -- in the tables above or not -- requires its Blueprint in hand (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}: Blueprints): buy it, reverse-engineer it from a Deconstruction, or author an original. A proven plan builds at the baseline; a degraded copy or an unproven original takes its penalty on every phase roll below.

  • A slugthrower round is two parts. A Casing -- the Bronzium shell, priced and weighed separately below, and the only part that survives firing -- loaded with a Shot Type: the Durasteel projectile with its Gunpowder propellant and any special processing the shot calls for (Standard, Hollow Point, AP and so on).
  • The Shot Type already includes its propellant charge. Nothing further is added before loading.
  • Either half can be built alone. A Casing can be cast empty and loaded later; a Shot Type can be crafted to load into an existing Casing, exactly as Handloading does with a recovered one. Building both together in one sitting is simply the default.
  • Cycler Rounds and Gauntlet Darts are different. Neither uses a reusable Casing, so the Casing and Shot Type split does not apply to them.

Skills Required:

  • Power Packs (Standard, Rifle, Heavy): Armoury (Small Arms) or Electronics Repair (Blasters) to assemble the physical casing, energy gates, and internal diodes.
  • Software Initialization (Power Packs): Any power pack requires a successful Computer Programming roll. This represents aligning the charge distribution matrix and calibrating the discharge rates to interface safely with the weapon. This is rolled after the physical assembly is complete.
  • Standard Projectiles (Slugs, Cycler Rounds, Darts): Armoury (Small Arms) or Machinist to cast, mill, and assemble the projectiles, primers, and kinetic payloads -- Casings specifically only apply to Slugthrower Pistol and Rifle rounds (see Casing/Shot Type, above); Cycler Rounds and Gauntlet Darts are built as complete, non-reloadable projectiles.
  • Special Projectiles (Hollow Point, AP, Incendiary, Explosive, Toxins): Constructing specialized ammunition requires the base assembly roll, plus an additional roll to properly seat the complex payload:
  • Hollow Point: Machinist (to precision-cut the expanding tips).
  • Armor-Piercing (AP): Machinist and Smith (to properly forge and harden the durasteel/bronzium core).
  • Incendiary / Explosive: Chemistry or Explosives (to synthesize and integrate the detonite, baradium, or other compounds without premature detonation).
  • Chemical / Toxin Darts (Paralysis, Synox, Venom): Chemistry or Poisons (to synthesize the payload and secure it in the micro-delivery delivery system).
  • Flamer Fuel Tanks: Armoury (Heavy Weapons) or Machinist to construct the pressurized tanks, valves, and reinforced seals.

Flamer Fuel Vendor Rule: Constructing a Flamer Fuel canister or tank yields an Empty Tank. Before it can be used, the crafter must either synthesize the highly volatile combustible gel themselves (requiring a successful Chemistry roll and raw chemical materials) or take the empty tank to a licensed vendor or quartermaster and pay the standard Refill Cost (e.g., 60 CR for a Small Canister, 300 CR for a Large Tank).

Base Time:

  • Hardware & Assembly (Projectiles): 10 minutes of labor per standard magazine, clip, or batch of darts (Slugthrower Pistol/Rifle: 5 minutes forming the Casing, 5 minutes loading a Standard or Nonlethal Shot Type). Special Shot Types (Hollow Point, AP, Incendiary) require 20 minutes per batch total -- still 5 minutes for the Casing, the remaining 15 minutes is the Shot Type’s own extra processing. A Casing or Shot Type crafted on its own, independent of a full round, takes only its own share of this time -- see Casing/Shot Type, above, and Handloading, below.
  • Hardware & Assembly (Power Packs & Tanks): 30 minutes of labor per power pack or empty flamer tank.
  • Software Initialization: 15 minutes of coding and system calibration for any power pack requiring a Computer Programming roll.
  • Chemical Synthesis: 30 minutes to synthesize the payload for special rounds, toxin darts, or flamer fuel.

Workspace Modifiers:

  • Improvised/Field Tools (-5 to skill): Using a vibro-knife, scavenged wire, a camp-heater, or a generic hydrospanner.
  • Basic Toolkit (-2 to skill): Using a portable armorer’s kit, a basic mechanic’s satchel, or standard field-cleaning kits.
  • Dedicated Workshop/Lab (+0 to skill): A facility specifically outfitted with a gunsmith’s bench, plasma welders, precision lathes, and dedicated diagnostic computers.
  • Advanced Research Facility (+2 to skill): Top-tier corporate weapons R&D labs (like Czerka or BlasTech), state-of-the-art military foundries, or elite Mandalorian forges.

Taking Extra Time:

  • Taking Extra Time: As @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10} (General Gear & Currency): double the base time for +1, four times for +2, eight times for +3, fifteen times for +4, thirty times for +5, whatever your tools.

Failure Conditions:

  • Hardware/Assembly (Physical): A failed assembly skill roll means the casing is malformed, the primer is dead, or the tank seal leaks; 50% of the raw materials are wasted and must be replaced before another attempt can be made. A critical failure destroys 100% of the materials and creates a “squib” or unstable component that will jam or misfire on the weapon’s next attack roll.
  • Chemistry/Explosives (Special Ammo & Fuel): A failed roll ruins the chemical batch; 50% of the raw materials are wasted. A critical failure results in an immediate localized explosion or toxic leak, inflicting the ammunition’s base damage directly to the crafter.
  • Software (Computer Programming): A failed Computer Programming roll means the power pack is physically intact but “bricked”—it cannot hold a charge or handshake with a weapon. No materials are wasted, but the crafter must spend another 15 minutes debugging and attempt a new roll. A critical failure creates a volatile cell: it functions normally at first, but automatically shorts out the weapon’s emitter on its first attack roll, disabling the weapon until repaired.

Ammunition Salvaging

Breaking down unneeded, damaged, or captured ammunition allows characters to reclaim valuable materials for future crafting endeavors.

Skills Required

  • Power Packs: Electronics Repair (Blasters) or Armoury (Small Arms) to safely discharge and disassemble the internal battery matrices and diode gates.
  • Standard Projectiles: Armoury (Small Arms) or Machinist to pull slugs, extract primers, and reclaim propellant without warping the Casing -- for Slugthrower Pistol/Rifle rounds, the Casing survives this process intact by design (see Yield Rates, below); Cycler Rounds and Gauntlet Darts have no Casing to preserve.
  • Special Projectiles & Fuel: Explosives (EOD) or Chemistry. Dismantling incendiary rounds, explosive payloads, toxic darts, or volatile flamer fuel requires highly specialized handling to avoid accidental release or detonation.

Base Time

  • Standard Munitions: 5 minutes per standard magazine, clip, or individual power pack.
  • Special Munitions: 15 minutes per batch of special projectiles, individual explosive round, or pressurized fuel tank due to the meticulous safety precautions required.

Yield Rates

  • Standard Success: The character safely extracts components, recovering 50% of the original raw material weight of the salvaged ammunition. For power packs, this yields reusable energy gates, wiring, and casing scrap. For Slugthrower Pistol/Rifle rounds specifically, the Casing is recovered fully intact (Casing Stats, in Handloading below) in addition to the 50%, which applies to the Shot Type portion only -- the projectile, propellant, and payload materials, not the shell. For Cycler Rounds, Gauntlet Darts, and other projectiles without a Casing, this yields usable metals and stable propellants from the whole round.
  • Critical Success: The character disassembles the ordnance with exceptional precision, recovering 75% of the raw material weight and preserving fully intact, reusable sub-components (such as a pristine hollow-point tip or an unblemished focusing diode). For Slugthrower Pistol/Rifle rounds, the Casing is recovered intact exactly as on a Standard Success (this does not change on a Critical Success -- there is only one Casing to recover); the 75% applies to the Shot Type portion.

Failure Conditions

  • Hardware Failure (Standard Munitions): A failed skill roll destroys the delicate components during disassembly. The materials are completely stripped, warped, or cracked, yielding no recoverable scrap -- this includes the Casing on Slugthrower Pistol/Rifle rounds; its intact preservation is only guaranteed on a Success or better, not a Failure.
  • Critical Failure (Standard Munitions): The armorer’s tools slip or a power cell matrix shorts out violently. All materials are destroyed, and the character takes minor localized damage (typically 1d-3 burn or crushing) from the feedback or sudden spring release.
  • Hazard Failure (Special Munitions): A failed roll ruins the volatile compounds or chemical binders, rendering them permanently inert and useless. No materials are recovered.
  • Hazard Critical Failure (Special Munitions): The explosive payload, chemical toxin, or volatile gel violently ignites or deploys during the dismantling process. The character is immediately subjected to the full base damage and secondary effects of the specific ammunition type.

Workspace Modifiers

  • Improvised Tools: -5 to skill. Attempting to dismantle explosives or power cells with scavenged tools is incredibly dangerous.
  • Basic Toolkit: -2 to skill.
  • Dedicated Workshop: +0 to skill.
  • Advanced Facility: +2 to skill.

Handloading

A cheaper, faster alternative to Crafting Ammunition from raw materials -- reusing a spent Casing rather than forging a new one. Applies to Slugthrower Pistol and Rifle rounds only, with any Shot Type loaded into the recovered Casing -- Standard, Hollow Point, AP, or any other Shot Type sharing that caliber’s Casing, since the Casing itself doesn’t care what was loaded into it last. Power Packs, Cycler Rounds, and Gauntlet Darts have no reusable Casing and cannot be Handloaded.

Requirement: One Casing per round handloaded -- recovered spent from a fired round (keep your own, or scavenge someone else’s) or bought/crafted fresh and empty (Casing Stats, below). Either way, Handloading only pays for the Shot Type, since the Casing itself is already on hand.

Casing Stats: Equal to the Bronzium line of that caliber’s Standard entry, above -- 0.02 lbs / 1 CR raw material for Pistol, 0.04 lbs / 1 CR for Rifle, at the ×2 of Phase 1, Armoury (IQ/Average): 2 CR Market Cost for either caliber. Same stats whether the Casing was recovered spent from a fired round or bought/crafted fresh and empty -- it’s the same physical shell either way. Sold and tracked the same way loose rounds are: per-unit weight and value, multiplied by quantity carried.

Shot Type Stats: Each caliber’s round entries, above, minus that caliber’s 2 CR Casing Market Cost -- the remainder is the Shot Type’s own Market Cost, sold and bought on its own. Weight is likewise the full round’s listed weight minus the Casing’s weight (i.e., everything except the Bronzium shell -- the projectile, whatever it’s made of, plus propellant and any special payload). Pistol: Standard 4 CR (0.03 lbs), Nonlethal 4 CR (0.03 lbs), Hollow Point 4 CR (0.029 lbs), AP 4 CR (0.04 lbs), Incendiary 14 CR (0.035 lbs). Rifle: Standard 4 CR (0.06 lbs), Nonlethal 4 CR (0.06 lbs), Hollow Point 4 CR (0.058 lbs), AP 4 CR (0.08 lbs), Incendiary 24 CR (0.07 lbs). The extra rolls that special Shot Types require (see Crafting Ammunition, above) gate who can craft them; they never change the price. Market price follows materials through the phase chain, so every Shot Type is its round’s Market Cost less the 2 CR Casing — Incendiary runs higher only because Baradium does.

Skill: Whatever the Shot Type being loaded normally calls for, above -- Armoury (Small Arms) or Machinist for Standard or Nonlethal, plus the Shot Type’s own additional roll if it has one (Machinist for Hollow Point; Machinist and Smith for AP; Machinist and Chemistry for Incendiary).

Material & Time: Load a Shot Type into the recovered Casing -- pay only the Shot Type’s own Market Cost (Shot Type Stats, above), skipping the Casing’s 2 CR entirely since it’s already on hand. Base Time is 5 minutes for Standard or Nonlethal, 15 minutes for Hollow Point, AP, or Incendiary (see Base Time, in Crafting Ammunition above) -- never the full 10 or 20 minute figure, since forming the Casing itself is skipped entirely.

Failure: As Crafting Ammunition’s Standard Projectiles (Hardware/Assembly Failure Conditions, above) -- a failed roll wastes 50% of the (already-discounted) materials and ruins the spent casing being reloaded.

Improvised Rounds

Field-expedient ammunition built from generic scrap rather than proper ammunition-grade components -- a survival measure, not a cost-saving one. Applies to Slugthrower Pistol, Rifle, and Cycler rounds -- basic kinetic slugs a generic metal scrap can plausibly substitute for. Gauntlet Darts do not qualify: their value comes from a specialized chemical, explosive, or toxin payload that scrap cannot replicate. Any generic, low-value metal object plausibly on hand qualifies as source material for the GM to describe -- pipe fittings, tool housings, vehicle paneling, droid chassis fragments, and the like. Not valid: non-metallic material, named or precious materials (Beskar, Phrik, Aurodium, Electrum, and similar), electronic or precision components (Silicon, circuitry), or a weapon/armor piece still in use by someone else -- that has to go through Salvaging or Deconstruct properly first, not skip straight to scrap.

Material: Scrap Metal (see the Materials table in @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}) at the same weight the Standard Projectiles entry, above, calls for -- no dedicated ammunition-crafting materials required.

Skill: Same as Standard Projectiles, above, but built using the Improvised/Field Tools workspace modifier (-5 to skill) regardless of what workspace is actually available -- makeshift construction imposes its own penalty.

Reliability: Improvised Rounds deal -1 damage and carry a 1-in-6 chance (roll 1 on 1d6) of misfiring harmlessly when fired -- no damage dealt, the round is wasted, and the weapon needs a Ready maneuver to clear before firing again.

Crafting Modifications for Ranged Weapons

This system governs the fabrication and installation of upgrades for existing ranged weapons. Modifications require precision and, depending on the complexity of the component, a firm grasp of both mechanics and advanced electronics.

Building from a Blueprint: Every item you build -- in the tables above or not -- requires its Blueprint in hand (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}: Blueprints): buy it, reverse-engineer it from a Deconstruction, or author an original. A proven plan builds at the baseline; a degraded copy or an unproven original takes its penalty on every phase roll below.

Skills Required:

  • Physical Hardware (Barrels, Stocks, Chassis, Triggers): Armoury (Blasters), Armoury (Small Arms) or Armoury (Heavy Weapons), matching the host weapon's family -- or the weapon's own Armstech specialty where it has one: Armstech (Bowcaster), Armstech (Liquid Projector), Armstech (Explosive Launcher) or Armstech (Gauntlet). Machinist may be used at a -2 penalty for fabrication of metal components, but cannot be used for complex trigger or gas-delivery mechanisms.
  • Electronics & Sensors (Optics, Smart-links, Programmed Triggers): Electronics Repair (Computers/Sensors) is required for optical systems and smart-linked targeting.
  • Blaster Power Systems (Power Cells, Emitters, Modulators): Electronics Repair (Blasters) is required for energy-based modifications.
  • Software Initialization (Silicon Requirement): Any modification containing Silicon (representing integrated targeting computers, electronic scopes, thermal regulators, or smart-link triggers) requires a successful Computer Programming roll. This is performed after physical installation to integrate the component with the weapon’s existing feed or fire system.

Base Time:

  • Physical Installation: 30 minutes of labor per modification slot required.
  • Software Initialization: 1 hour of coding and system calibration for any component requiring a Computer Programming roll.

Workspace Modifiers:

  • Improvised/Field Tools (-5 to skill): Using scavenged parts, a multi-tool, or improvised workbenches.
  • Basic Toolkit (-2 to skill): Using a portable armorer’s kit or field-repair satchel.
  • Dedicated Workshop/Lab (+0 to skill): A facility equipped with a gunsmith’s bench, precision tools, and diagnostic scanners.
  • Advanced Research Facility (+2 to skill): Corporate R&D labs or military-grade weapon testing facilities.

Taking Extra Time:

  • Taking Extra Time: As @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10} (General Gear & Currency): double the base time for +1, four times for +2, eight times for +3, fifteen times for +4, thirty times for +5, whatever your tools.

Failure Conditions:

  • Physical Installation: A failed roll means the component is improperly seated or mounted, rendering it non-functional and potentially damaging the mounting slot; 50% of the raw material cost is wasted. A critical failure damages the host weapon itself, imposing a -1 penalty to the weapon’s accuracy or HT until a successful repair roll is made.
  • Software (Computer Programming): A failed Computer Programming roll results in a “bricked” component. The physical modification is secure, but the software fails to handshake with the weapon’s internal bus. No materials are wasted, but the crafter must spend another hour debugging and attempt a new roll. A critical failure introduces a “ghost” glitch: the modification seems to work, but the weapon will jam or malfunction on a roll of 17 or 18.

Installing Ranged Modifications

Installing a modification requires precision. Misaligning a scope is frustrating, but improperly wiring an overcharge capacitor can be lethal.

Skills Required

  • Physical Hardware (Stocks, Receivers, Muzzles): Armoury (Blasters), Armoury (Small Arms) or Armoury (Heavy Weapons), matching the host weapon's family -- or the weapon's own Armstech specialty where it has one: Armstech (Bowcaster), Armstech (Liquid Projector), Armstech (Explosive Launcher) or Armstech (Gauntlet). Machinist may be used at a -2 penalty for basic mounts.
  • Blaster Power Systems (Power Cells, Emitters): Electronics Repair (Blasters).
  • Optics & Sensors (Scopes, Rangefinders): Electronics Repair (Computers/Sensors).
  • Software Integration (Silicon Requirement): Any modification containing Silicon (Targeting Links, Burst Modules) requires a Computer Programming roll to “handshake” the component with the weapon’s internal bus.

Base Time & Workspace

  • Physical Installation: 30 minutes of careful labor per modification slot occupied.
  • Software Initialization: 1 hour of coding and system calibration.
  • Modifiers:
  • Improvised/Field Tools: -5 to skill.
  • Basic Toolkit: -2 to skill.
  • Dedicated Workshop/Lab: +0 to skill.
  • Advanced Research Facility: +2 to skill.

Failure Consequences

Physical Installation Failures

  • Standard Failure: The component is improperly seated or the mounting rails are warped. The modification is non-functional, and 50% of the raw material cost used to build the mod is wasted (if newly crafted) or the mod requires a 30-minute repair.
  • Critical Failure: A catastrophic slip damages the host weapon. The weapon suffers a -1 penalty to Acc or HT (GM’s discretion based on the part) until a successful Armoury repair roll is made.

Software Integration Failures

  • Standard Failure: The component is “bricked.” The physical mount is secure, but the firmware rejects the upgrade. No materials are wasted, but the crafter must spend another hour debugging and attempt a new Computer Programming roll before the mod functions.
  • Critical Failure: The dreaded “ghost glitch.” The modification appears to work perfectly upon testing. However, the weapon will completely jam, short out, or suffer a power overload on an attack roll of 17 or 18 during combat.

Uninstalling Ranged Modifications

There is a distinct difference between carefully removing a scope to put it on a new sniper rifle, and tearing a busted rifle apart for scrap metal and silicon.

Clean Uninstall

Carefully detaching, or undoing a working modification so it can be reused on another weapon.

  • Skills Required: The same skill used to install the item (e.g., Armoury or Electronics Repair). No Computer Programming roll is needed unless the user wishes to wipe the memory core clean.
  • Base Time: 15 minutes of labor per modification slot.
  • Success: The component is removed flawlessly, or the weapon is returned to its default state, and can be immediately installed on another compatible weapon.
  • Failure: The component’s mounting bracket is sheared or a delicate wire is snapped. The component is broken and must be repaired before it can be reinstalled.
  • Critical Failure: The component is completely destroyed during removal.

Grenades and other explosives offer area-of-effect damage. They are typically thrown weapons, but mines are placed and triggered by proximity, timers, or tripwires.

Legality Class (LC): The LC column on the tables below says how hard a thing is to obtain lawfully, and it is the only place in this book where that is a number rather than a matter for the GM.

  • LC 1 is banned outright in civilised space -- possession alone is a crime, and acquisition means the black market and a Streetwise roll at -2.
  • Nothing here is LC 0, which would be something no one sells at any price.

Salvaging Ranged Weapon Modifications

Breaking down obsolete, damaged, or scavenged ranged weapon modifications allows characters to reclaim useful raw materials, delicate optics, and silicon components for future fabrication or repairs.

Skills Required:

  • Physical Hardware (Barrels, Stocks, Chassis, Triggers): Armoury (Blasters), Armoury (Small Arms) or Armoury (Heavy Weapons), matching the host weapon's family -- or the weapon's own Armstech specialty where it has one: Armstech (Bowcaster), Armstech (Liquid Projector), Armstech (Explosive Launcher) or Armstech (Gauntlet). Machinist may be used at a -2 penalty to carefully detach and break down metal components without warping them.
  • Electronics & Sensors (Optics, Smart-links, Programmed Triggers): Electronics Repair (Computers/Sensors) to safely detach and preserve delicate optical arrays and sensor suites.
  • Blaster Power Systems (Power Cells, Emitters, Modulators): Electronics Repair (Blasters) to properly discharge and extract energy-based components.
  • Software & Silicon Extraction: Computer Programming or Electronics Repair. Required if the modification contains Silicon (integrated targeting computers, electronic scopes, smart-link triggers) to safely extract the hardware without “bricking” the electronics.

Base Time:

  • Hardware Extraction: 15 minutes of continuous labor per modification slot the component occupies.
  • Software Extraction: 15 minutes of dedicated data-wiping and component isolation for modifications containing Silicon.

Yield Rates:

  • Standard Success: The character safely extracts and strips the modification, recovering 50% of its original raw material and silicon weight.
  • Critical Success: The character disassembles the modification with expert precision, recovering 75% of its raw material weight and preserving a fully intact, reusable sub-component (such as an unblemished focusing lens or a pristine targeting sensor).

Failure Conditions:

  • Hardware Failure (Physical): A failed skill roll ruins the delicate components during extraction. Lenses are scratched, metal mounts are warped, and power couplings are sheared. The modification is reduced to useless junk, yielding no recoverable materials.
  • Critical Hardware Failure: A power cell shorts out or a pressurized valve bursts during removal. All materials from the modification are destroyed, and the salvager takes minor localized damage (1d-3 burning, piercing, or crushing). If the modification was still attached to a host weapon, the host weapon suffers a -1 penalty to its accuracy or HT until a successful repair roll is made.
  • Software Failure (Silicon Extraction): A failed Computer Programming roll “bricks” the modification’s electronic components. The physical scrap can still be salvaged via the appropriate hardware roll, but no Silicon weight is recovered.

Workspace Modifiers:

  • Improvised/Field Tools (-5 to skill): Using scavenged parts, a multi-tool, or improvised workbenches.
  • Basic Toolkit (-2 to skill): Using a portable armorer’s kit or field-repair satchel.
  • Dedicated Workshop/Lab (+0 to skill): A facility equipped with a gunsmith’s bench, precision tools, and diagnostic scanners.
  • Advanced Research Facility (+2 to skill): Corporate R&D labs or military-grade weapon testing facilities.

Crafting Explosives:

Crafting explosives is a high-risk endeavor. A stable explosive requires careful chemical synthesis, while proximity triggers, timers, and the arming sequences demand delicate electronic and software calibration.

Building from a Blueprint: Every item you build -- in the tables above or not -- requires its Blueprint in hand (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}: Blueprints): buy it, reverse-engineer it from a Deconstruction, or author an original. A proven plan builds at the baseline; a degraded copy or an unproven original takes its penalty on every phase roll below.

Skills Required

  • Chemical Synthesis (Explosives & Payloads): Alchemy (if specialized in explosives) or Chemistry (to stabilize compounds like Baradium or Synox).
  • Hardware & Trigger Assembly: Armoury (Explosives) or Demolitions (to build the casing and mechanical trigger mechanism).
  • Electronics Integration: Electronics Repair (Security) or Electronics Repair (Cybernetics) is required to wire proximity or laser trip triggers into the detonator.
  • Software Initialization (Silicon & Diatium Requirement): Computer Programming is mandatory to configure the Silicon logic boards and regulate the Diatium power cells. This roll ensures the arming button functions properly and the electronic sequence does not misfire.

Base Time & Workspace

  • Chemical Synthesis: 2 hours per pound of explosive compound to stabilize and package.
  • Hardware & Electronics Assembly: 1 hour to assemble the casing and wire the physical trigger.
  • Software Initialization: 30 minutes of coding and diagnostic testing to sync the electronic detonator.
  • Workspace Modifiers:
  • Improvised/Field Tools: -5 to skill (High risk of premature detonation).
  • Basic Toolkit: -2 to skill.
  • Dedicated Workshop/Forge: +0 to skill.
  • Advanced Research Facility: +2 to skill.

Failure Consequences

  • Synthesis Failures:
  • Standard Failure: The explosive is inert or “damp.” The materials are wasted, and the crafter must clean the workspace to prevent residue contamination before starting over.
  • Critical Failure: The compound becomes hyper-volatile. The crafter must immediately make a DX roll or take 2d burning damage as the compound flashes off.
  • Trigger/Assembly Failures:
  • Standard Failure: The physical trigger fails to arm. The device is non-functional; the crafter must spend 1 hour disassembling and re-wiring the trigger.
  • Critical Failure: The device is “hot.” It arms prematurely. The crafter must succeed on a DX roll to jettison the device before it detonates in their hands.
  • Software Initialization Failures:
  • Standard Failure: The logic board fails to sync with the detonator. The explosive is physically sound but will not arm; the crafter must spend 30 minutes debugging the code and attempt a new roll.
  • Critical Failure: The firmware enters a feedback loop, shorting out the Diatium power cell and permanently bricking the Silicon logic board. Both the Diatium and Silicon components are ruined and must be replaced.

Salvaging Explosives:

Recovering explosives is often more dangerous than crafting them. You are dealing with volatile compounds that have been subjected to combat stress, environmental degradation, and potential damage.

Skills Required

  • Extraction: Demolitions or Electronics Repair (to deactivate the trigger before salvaging the payload).
  • Chemical Recovery: Chemistry (to safely remove the explosive compound from the casing).

Base Time

  • 30 minutes to carefully deactivate the trigger mechanism.
  • 60 minutes to safely extract the explosive payload.

Yield Rates

  • Standard Success: You recover 50% of the raw material weight (Baradium, Detonite, etc.) in a stable enough form to be safely re-used.
  • Critical Success: You recover 75% of the raw material weight. You also salvage a functioning, pristine trigger module (timer or proximity).
  • Failure Conditions:
  • Deactivation Failure: A failed Demolitions roll triggers the device. The explosive detonates immediately.
  • Chemical Failure: A failed Chemistry roll ruins the explosive compound, rendering it useless and potentially toxic (1d-3 toxic damage if handled without gloves).
  • Critical Failure: A “Total Detonation.” All materials are vaporized. The salvager takes 3d damage and is stunned for 1d-3 minutes.
